profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap record, tagged Verizon Wireless Mew Building, sits in Southlake, Tarrant County, Texas near Kirkwood Boulevard. The name itself signals wireless-network infrastructure rather than commercial colocation space, consistent with a mobile switching center or radio-network equipment site supporting Verizon cellular service in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. The word Mew in the name could not be explained by any source consulted this session. No nearby street, subdivision, or landmark by that name was found, so it may be an internal Verizon building code, a data-entry artifact from whatever source the original mapper used, or something else not documented anywhere accessible. More notable is how the telecom=data_center tag was added to this record: the edit history shows it was added inside a much larger changeset of 362 individual changes whose own changeset comment reads only added houses, indicating the edit was very likely part of a bulk residential-housing mapping pass and that the data-center tag on this particular way was added incidentally or by mistake rather than as a deliberate, sourced classification. This is the weakest tag provenance found anywhere in this Verizon record cluster alongside the Sandy City, Utah MapRoulette tag. Texas is outside the nine-state footprint where Verizon operates as the legacy incumbent local exchange carrier, so no regional Bell heritage explanation applies here. Given both the unexplained building name and the accidental-looking tagging history, this record should be treated as unconfirmed and possibly mistagged rather than a verified data center, and no capacity, square footage, tier rating, or year-built figures are asserted.

sources.title: Equinix Completes Acquisition of 29 Data Centers from Verizon

profile.research_note: Verizon sold its commercial colocation/data-center business (29 facilities) to Equinix in 2017 and exited the public colocation market; it does not publish colocation spec sheets. These rows are Verizon-operated network facilities (switching centers, wireless MSC/central-office buildings) rather than for-lease colocation space, and no public technical spec page exists for them. Marked specs_unpublished rather than guess.

reading.body:
This facility is a Verizon wireless network building near Kirkwood Boulevard in Southlake, Tarrant County, not a commercial data center. Verizon exited the public colocation market in 2017 when it sold 29 facilities to Equinix, and it publishes no technical specifications for its remaining network infrastructure. The data center tag on this OpenStreetMap record was added as part of a bulk residential housing mapping pass and appears to be a mistake rather than a deliberate classification.

No capacity figures, power consumption, square footage, or tier rating are published for this facility. Without public specifications from the operator, it cannot be ranked by power draw or computing potential. Its role in supporting Verizon's cellular network in the Dallas-Fort Worth region is consistent with its building name and location, but this tells nothing about any contribution to AI workloads.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which 19 have published power ratings totaling 475 MW. This facility holds no confirmed position in that published capacity because no spec page exists to read. It should not be treated as verified infrastructure relevant to AI scaling decisions.
